sections.overview: The Eurasian chaffinch is a small, widespread finch whose continental range extends from Europe eastward through temperate Asia. AviList 2025b treats Fringilla coelebs as distinct from the African, Azores, Madeira and Canary Islands chaffinches; the Tenerife and Gran Canaria Blue Chaffinches are separate species too. Many populations are resident, while birds from northern and eastern breeding areas move south or west for winter.
sections.identification: Breeding males have a blue-grey crown, rosy face and breast, chestnut back, and two white wing bars. The male’s pinkish-orange breast becomes a darker wine shade in winter, a subtle seasonal change within the same male pattern. The female and juvenile are softer brown and olive tones; their pale wing bars and white outer tail feathers remain useful clues in flight. The RSPB lists a typical adult length of 14.5 cm, a weight range of 18–29 g, and a wingspan of 24.5–28.5 cm. In British ringing samples, males average 22.6 g and females 20.9 g, against 21.8 g for adults overall.
sections.habitat: In Britain, chaffinches occupy deciduous, mixed and coniferous woodland during breeding and also visit open farmland in winter.
sections.diet: Outside breeding, adults pick seeds from the ground and rarely take them directly from plants; in spring and summer they also glean insects from shrub and tree foliage. They feed nestlings invertebrates, including caterpillars, spiders, crane flies, aphids, and beetles, shifting the young diet toward animal prey.
sections.behavior: During spring, males sing from exposed perches and defend breeding territories; the familiar song descends through a short sequence and ends in a flourish. Chaffinch song is learned from adult tutors, and neighbouring populations develop distinct song dialects through cultural transmission. Outside the territorial season, birds feed in loose flocks, sometimes alongside Bramblings and other finches; migration is partial, with northern and eastern birds moving while many western birds stay year-round.
sections.reproduction: The female builds a compact, deep cup in a tree or shrub fork, weaving moss, grass, roots, lichens, bark, hair, and feathers together. In Britain, laying begins on average around 30 April; a typical clutch contains four or five eggs, incubated by the female for about 12–13 days. The female feeds nestlings caterpillars and other animal food; after they leave the nest, the male also helps provision the young for about three weeks. BTO nest records show that chicks usually fledge at 13–15.5 days.
sections.ecology: On nine south-central English farms, adults made little use of crops when feeding nestlings; trees and hedges, especially oaks and willows, were frequent feeding sites. Successful nests tended to be nearer oaks or willows than nests where chicks starved; in one study year, starvation was less frequent along field boundaries with oak trees.
sections.conservation: The IUCN assessment, last assessed on 9 August 2018 and published as an amended 2019 version, listed the then broadly defined Common Chaffinch as Least Concern and reported an increasing global population trend at that time; its preliminary population estimate still required validation. That assessment predates the current separation of several island and North African chaffinch species, so it should not be read as a fresh assessment of every present-day taxon. In the UK, the BTO records a 26% breeding decline (1967–2024), though the species remains Green on the UK Birds of Conservation Concern list; numbers have fallen in all four countries since about 2010 after late-century growth. Trichomonosis, a contagious protozoan disease, has been linked to the downturn, but BTO researchers say its role in the sharper recent decline remains uncertain.
